To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the recorded diagnosis of atopic dermatitis in a sample of insured dogs was considered valid, but that many dogs with a recorded CAD diagnosis had been treated for a cutaneous adverse food reaction before the diagnosis of CAD was made.

the recorded diagnosis of CAD in the insurance database was valid in 97.6% of the included individuals, but that the proportion of individuals that were truly atopy could not be determined due to the lack of information regarding dietary trial in many dogs.

1) the agreement between the reported diagnosis of CAD in the insurance database (i.e. based on information submitted by the attending veterinarian) and the clinical manifestations in the submitted medical record was considered acceptable, but 2) many attending veterinarians apparently did not exclude cutural adverse food reactions (CAFR) before making the diagnosis CAD.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the validation of a recorded diagnosis in an insurance database, which is an approach rarely used.
the validation of the insurance database as a tool for studying CAD, as well as with the prevalence of this disease in the insured dog population.

the validation of the insurance database as a source for information regarding CAD in a population of dogs with a recorded CAD diagnosis, and the evaluation of the clinical characteristics of dogs that respond to dietary trial testing.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the diagnosis of CAD was made correctly in the majority of the dogs included in the present study.
the diagnosis of CAD is made in a substantial proportion of Swedish dogs with skin disease, but that the diagnosis may not always be correct.
a large proportion of insured Swedish dogs diagnosed with CAD had some allergic skin disease, but that the true proportion that were atopic is unknown.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the diagnosis of CAD is validated, but that the clinical picture of CAD may be confounded by the presence of cutaneous adverse food reaction.
the diagnosis of CAD in the insurance database was considered to be correct in most cases, but the diagnostic workup was not complete enough in many dogs.
the recorded diagnosis in our insurance database was considered valid, but that the diagnosis of CAD should be made with caution.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many dogs that could be considered atopic but that have not been subjected to a thorough diagnostic workup to confirm this diagnosis.
the diagnosis of atopic dermatitis is not as straightforward as many veterinarians think.
the diagnosis of CAD is not made on the basis of a single positive intradermal test reaction, but rather on the basis of the clinical picture and a positive response to treatment.
